idiom_name: ADO.NET DbDataAdapter + DataTable (or Dapper methods over IDbConnection)
implementation_notes: System.Data ships the pattern: one DbDataAdapter per table carries SelectCommand/InsertCommand/UpdateCommand/DeleteCommand, Fill() materialises a DataTable whose DataRow instances are the records, and Update() writes changed rows back through the same gateway - connection pooling, provider differences and generated keys are handled by ADO.NET, so the classic structure needs no hand-written shell. The modern shorthand keeps identical semantics with less machinery: a sealed class whose methods run parameterized statements over IDbConnection and map rows to POCOs (Dapper, or DbCommand/DbDataReader by hand). Prefer the DataSet/DataAdapter form for offline or batch synchronisation and data-bound UI, where row state and UpdateBatchSize come for free; prefer the POCO form for services.
pitfalls: DbDataAdapter.Update skips rows whose RowState is Unchanged or that lack a primary key, so a missed AcceptChanges looks like a silently lost write.
DataTable is not thread-safe; caching one across requests turns a per-request bug into a data race.
ADO.NET pools connections, so open per call and let the pool do its job - a single shared DbConnection serialises or breaks concurrent calls.
Parameter names in SQL must match the anonymous-object/Dapper member names exactly; a typo becomes a runtime error only on the paths that execute.
